Test Case: Send DELETE /v3/project/{id} for a project that exists in the caller's region+owner scope
Expected Result: Response status is 200 and the body is {deleted: true, id: <the requested id>}

Test Case: Inspect the 200 response body's `id` field after deleting project P
Expected Result: The `id` equals P's id exactly, so the caller can confirm which project was removed

Test Case: Send DELETE /v3/project/{id} for an id that does not exist in the store
Expected Result: Response status is 404 and no record in the store is modified

Test Case: Delete project P successfully, then send DELETE for P a second time
Expected Result: The second request returns 404 — not 200 — because P no longer exists to any scoped read

Test Case: Compare the first and second DELETE responses for the same project id
Expected Result: The endpoint is not idempotent: first 200, second 404. A 200 on the second call would falsely report deleting something this request did not delete

Test Case: Force the project record write to fail, then send DELETE for a valid in-scope project
Expected Result: Response status is 500

Test Case: Force the export-folder removal to fail, then send DELETE for a valid in-scope project whose folder exists
Expected Result: Response status is 200 (not 500): the record is already marked deleted by that point, so the delete has succeeded from the caller's point of view; the orphaned folder is logged instead

Test Case: Send DELETE /v3/project/{id} with no session token
Expected Result: Response status is 401 and the project is not deleted

Test Case: Send DELETE /v3/project/{id} with a token signed by the wrong secret
Expected Result: Response status is 401 and the project is not deleted

Test Case: As a caller scoped to region NA / owner u1, send DELETE for a live project owned by region EU / owner u2
Expected Result: Response status is 404 and the target project's isDeleted remains false

Test Case: Compare the 404 response for an unknown id with the 404 response for a project outside the caller's scope
Expected Result: Both responses are identical in status and body, so the response cannot be used to discover whether another operator's project exists

Test Case: Send DELETE with a region and owner supplied in the query string that differ from those in the session token
Expected Result: The query-string values are ignored; the scope used is the one derived from the token

Test Case: Delete project P, then read P's raw record from the store
Expected Result: P.isDeleted is true

Test Case: Count the records in the store before and after deleting project P
Expected Result: The record count is unchanged — the row is flagged, not removed

Test Case: Delete project P and compare P.updated_at before and after
Expected Result: P.updated_at is refreshed to the deletion time

Test Case: Delete project P, then request the project list for the same scope
Expected Result: P is absent from the returned list

Test Case: Delete project P, then request P by its id
Expected Result: Response status is 404

Test Case: Store a destination management token for project P (so P.destinationToken.secretEncrypted is set), then delete P and read the raw record
Expected Result: P.destinationToken.secretEncrypted still holds its original value — the deletion writes the isDeleted field only and does not replace the record wholesale

Test Case: Delete project P and compare every other field on P's record before and after (name, description, source, graph, audit, contentTypeSelection)
Expected Result: Only isDeleted and updated_at differ; every other field is byte-identical

Test Case: With two live projects P and Q in the same scope, delete P and inspect Q
Expected Result: Q.isDeleted is false and Q is still returned by the project list

Test Case: Delete project P whose export folder exportData/<P.id>/ contains at least one file
Expected Result: exportData/<P.id>/ no longer exists

Test Case: Delete project P whose export folder contains nested content (a branch subfolder, content_types/, entries/<ct>/<locale>/, assets/files/<uid>/<filename>)
Expected Result: The whole tree under exportData/<P.id>/ is gone, including every nested directory and file

Test Case: Delete project P whose export folder contains an audit findings cache file
Expected Result: The cache file is removed along with the folder; no audit cache for P survives on disk

Test Case: Delete project P that has never been exported, so exportData/<P.id>/ does not exist
Expected Result: Response status is 200 and P.isDeleted is true — a missing folder is the desired end state, not an error

Test Case: With projects P and Q each having their own export folder, delete P and inspect Q's folder
Expected Result: exportData/<Q.id>/ still exists with all of its contents intact

Test Case: Make the export-folder removal fail (filesystem rejects the operation), then delete project P
Expected Result: P.isDeleted is true — the record is marked before the folder is touched, so P never remains live with its data already destroyed

Test Case: Observe the order of operations during a successful deletion
Expected Result: The project record write completes before the folder removal begins

Test Case: Delete a project whose id contains path-traversal characters (for example '../../../../etc')
Expected Result: No directory outside exportData/ is removed; the resolved target stays inside exportData/

Test Case: Delete a project whose id is empty or consists only of dots
Expected Result: The exportData/ root itself is not removed and remains a directory

Test Case: After deleting project P, list the exportData/ root
Expected Result: Only exportData/<P.id>/ was removed; every sibling project directory is still present

Test Case: Delete project P and observe outbound calls to Contentstack
Expected Result: No Contentstack Management API call is made — deletion affects this tool's own record and its export folder only, never the source stack

Test Case: Delete project P, then attempt to persist a source selection against P
Expected Result: The write is rejected with status 404 and P's stored source is unchanged

Test Case: Delete project P, then attempt to persist a content graph against P
Expected Result: The write is rejected with status 404 and P's stored graph is unchanged

Test Case: Delete project P, then attempt to persist audit include/exclude decisions against P
Expected Result: The write is rejected with status 404 and P's stored audit decisions are unchanged

Test Case: Delete project P, then attempt to persist a destination management token against P
Expected Result: The write is rejected with status 404 and P's stored destinationToken is unchanged

Test Case: Delete project P, then attempt to persist a content type selection against P
Expected Result: The write is rejected with status 404 (pre-existing behaviour, asserted here as a regression guard)

Test Case: For a LIVE project, perform each of the five writes above
Expected Result: All five succeed, confirming the guard rejects only deleted projects

Test Case: Delete project P, attempt any of the five writes, then read the project list
Expected Result: P remains absent from the list — a rejected write cannot bring a deleted project back into view

Test Case: Start an export for project P, delete P before the job reaches its final write, then let the job finish
Expected Result: No content graph is persisted for P

Test Case: Start an export for project P, delete P mid-export, then inspect the filesystem after the job ends
Expected Result: exportData/<P.id>/ does not exist — the job's final move does not recreate the folder the deletion removed

Test Case: Delete project P after its export has written its temporary working folder but before the folder is moved into place
Expected Result: The temporary working folder is also removed, leaving no partial export on disk

Test Case: Run an export to completion for a project that is NOT deleted
Expected Result: The export folder is finalised and the content graph is persisted as normal
